title: The Motivation to Help Others Succeed
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article argues that the best leaders derive genuine satisfaction from watching others succeed, treating team members' accomplishments as equal to or greater than their own, a motivation the author says is surprisingly uncommon rather than universal among leaders. It links this trait to compassion, empathy, and social intelligence, noting that leaders low in relational skill rarely invest in developing others. The piece also makes a practical case: leaders known for developing talent attract the most talented people, who in turn build trust faster and treat feedback as a gift rather than an attack. It closes with a Martin Luther King quote framing the drive to help others as central to what defines exceptional leadership.
points: Genuine investment in others' success is correlated with compassion, empathy, and social intelligence, not a universal leadership trait.
Team members who work under a development-focused leader tend to treat feedback as a gift rather than a threat, improving performance.
Leaders known for developing talent attract the most talented people, creating a self-reinforcing cycle of investment and attraction.
The article frames the motivation to develop others as starting in personal character but yielding measurable organizational benefits.
quotes: The best leaders are highly motivated to help others succeed.
But ask a great leader about their performance and they are more likely to point to the accomplishments of their team members than they are to their own outcomes.
Those leaders with strong relationship skills and social intelligence are more likely to invest in the success of others and find satisfaction in their accomplishments.
Those who work with a leader motivated to help them succeed treat feedback as a gift rather than as a bee sting.
In the words of Martin Luther King: “Life’s most persistent and urgent question is, ‘What are you doing for others?
